extracted.intended_audience: lawyers, tribunal staff, government trade officials, and industry participants involved in Canadian anti-dumping proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for the conduct of Canadian anti-dumping investigations and Tribunal inquiries, covering preliminary determinations, questionnaires, hearings, confidentiality, timetables, findings, reviews, and appeals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary exporter questionnaire
rubrics_metrics.description: Preliminary questionnaire inquiring into the nature of the exporter's business precedes a 'Request'. The response allows Special Assessment Programs to construct an appropriate subsequent 'Request'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to gather necessary background before requesting further information; forms the basis for constructing subsequent targeted requests to exporters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of undisclosed overseas verification procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Some overseas 'verification' of information supplied by exporters is carried out according to procedures that National Revenue will not disclose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledges existence of non-public verification methods; implies limited transparency about certain verification steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallback methods when insufficient information or state-controlled economies
rubrics_metrics.description: If the Deputy Minister cannot gather sufficient information to determine normal or export price, or if the goods have been exported to Canada from a state-controlled economy, he may use section 11 or subsection 9(7) of the Act to prescribe another method of determination — for example, based on the value for another exporter of the same goods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ministerial prescriptions may be issued as 'stand-by' measures to cover new models or exporters not part of the original investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Periods under review for preliminary determination
rubrics_metrics.description: The Deputy Minister examines the most recent figures on entries into Canada — typically figures for a six month period falling in the twelve months preceding initiation. To establish normal value, foreign domestic sales are examined generally on the basis of at least a sixty day period preceding sales to Canada. These two periods together constitute the 'period under review' for the purposes of a preliminary determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines temporal scope: ~6-month entry data and ≥60-day domestic sales window before Canadian sales; important for calculating margins and evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Termination criteria after investigation
rubrics_metrics.description: If there is insufficient evidence of dumping, or dumping is negligible, the proceedings are terminated. If dumping is found but no evidence of injury, proceedings will either be terminated or the injury question referred to the Tribunal under section 13.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies outcomes depending on evidence of dumping and injury; referral to Tribunal only when injury issue requires adjudication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional duties after preliminary determination
rubrics_metrics.description: Following a preliminary determination, the Deputy Minister assesses provisional duties against the dumped goods. Importers either pay provisional duty equal to the margin of dumping or post security in an equal amount. Dumped goods imported into Canada between the date of the preliminary determination and the date of the Tribunal's order or finding are entered provisionally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provisional duty is tied to the preliminary margin; provisional entries are allowed but duties/security required pending final outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reception of informal representations during investigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Throughout the investigation there will likely be attempts by complainant and the object of the complaint to make representations on dumping and injury, generally by counsel and largely informal, perhaps by telephone. It is reported that National Revenue is unsympathetic to such representations, particularly those made by exporters and importers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical note that informal outreach to National Revenue has limited effect; formal submissions through established procedures are preferable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden on domestic industry to initiate proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Domestic producers generally have the burden of initiating the process and supplying much of the necessary information, and must normally wait about seven months before a preliminary determination is made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognizes resource burden on complainant industry; justification offered: anti-dumping measures are exceptional and high demands are defensible from a free trade perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fast Track anti-dumping investigations (steel)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'Fast Track' system for imported steel: a Steel Task Force establishes Canadian 'bench-mark' prices; export prices below these attract attention and the Task Force will initiate a formal investigation if there is prima facie evidence of injury. The formal investigation period is three months rather than six, and ministerial prescriptions under section 11 will frequently be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example of expedited procedure in a perceived special need for protection—shorter deadlines and greater ministerial intervention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus of National Revenue on dumping over injury
rubrics_metrics.description: The major thrust of National Revenue's investigation is directed towards dumping, rather than injury; little attention appears to be paid even to the existence of prima facie injury. The justification is the Tribunal's responsibility for injury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This division can lead to cumbersome investigations for exporters/importers when evidence of harm is minimal; highlights systemic bias/tension in roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice of Commencement and service list (Rule 7 & 8)
rubrics_metrics.description: Following receipt of a preliminary determination, the Tribunal publishes a Notice of Commencement of Inquiry in the Canada Gazette, giving details and procedures for filing briefs and written submissions (Rule 7). Copies of the Notice are sent to importers and exporters, the government of the country of export, relevant trade associations, and the complainant (Rule 8).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies formal notice duties and whom the Tribunal must notify; important for procedural fairness and participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deputy Minister's filing obligations with Tribunal (Rule 9)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Deputy Minister files with the Tribunal the complaint, if any, and all relevant information provided by the complainant; in the absence of a complainant, the evidence relied on to find dumping and injury; a description of the dumped goods; information on Canadian production and on importation; and information on dumping and margin of dumping (Rule 9).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sets the content the Tribunal will receive from National Revenue to form the case record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timetable and statutory 90-day limit (subsection 16(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: The Secretary establishes a timetable for the inquiry. Subsection 16(3) of the Act requires the Tribunal to complete its work within 90 days. The Tribunal adheres to a strict timetable, which places the hearing at about the 45 day mark.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Time constraints shape all research, questionnaire, and hearing scheduling; Tribunal practice centers hearing roughly midway through the 90-day window.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice of Appearance timing (Rule 14)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any party who proposes to appear at the hearing must file a Notice of Appearance at least twenty days prior to the date fixed for the hearing (Rule 14); there appears to be no restriction on who may appear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sets procedural deadline for participation and openness of standing to appear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panel assignment by Chairman
rubrics_metrics.description: The Tribunal Chairman assigns three Tribunal members to the panel for the case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard composition for the adjudicative panel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Researcher preparation and questionnaires
rubrics_metrics.description: Assigned researcher visits the Ministry of National Revenue to discuss basis of complaint, the product, and other relevant matters; the researcher prepares and dispatches questionnaires for the Canadian industry and importers. The Canadian industry questionnaire focuses on the criteria for injury (production and sales figures, accounts lost, price reductions, inventory, employment, capacity and utilization). The importers' questionnaire concentrates on import activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Questionnaire system developed as part of 1974 reorganization; central to Tribunal fact-finding on injury and import patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Staff assembly of statistical information and field visits
rubrics_metrics.description: While waiting for questionnaire returns, staff assembles statistical information (particularly from Statistics Canada) on imports, production, employment and other relevant matters; visits complainants, other large producers and significant importers to discuss products and figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Triangulation of data sources; active fieldwork to understand industry context and verify questionnaire returns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Members' plant visits without discussing merits
rubrics_metrics.description: Members of the panel will likely visit the plants of Canadian producers to acquaint themselves with the product; care is taken, in the course of such visits, not to discuss the merits of the case. The occasional practice of meeting privately with the parties prior to the hearing to discuss the merits was abandoned after the Magnasonic decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plant visits allowed for factual familiarization but must avoid ex parte discussions about merits to respect natural justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose and conduct of preliminary sitting (Rule 15)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'preliminary sitting' is held to consider procedure to be followed at the hearing; to exchange briefs, documents and exhibits proposed to be submitted; to consider confidentiality problems; and to arrange for 'the expeditious presentation of evidence and the disposition of the inquiry' (Rule 15). The Tribunal may direct parties to appear at this sitting; those who plan to appear at the hearing almost always come.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preliminary sitting is logistical and procedural — not a merits hearing — and facilitates efficient use of hearing time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality marking and Tribunal discretion (Rule 12 & section 29(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: Persons submitting briefs, written submissions or exhibits may indicate that they are confidential; Section 29(3) requires the Tribunal to respect confidentiality in certain instances. If the Tribunal does not agree the submission is confidential, the person who submitted it may withdraw it (if done voluntarily). Prior to or at the commencement of a hearing, the Tribunal provides each person who has filed a Notice of Appearance with all information filed except that considered to be confidential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balancing confidentiality with procedural fairness; submitters may flag confidentiality but Tribunal has final say and must provide non-confidential material to parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closed-door handling of confidential evidence (Rule 24)
rubrics_metrics.description: When confidential information will be given in evidence, the Tribunal goes behind closed doors, excluding everyone except the various counsel (and any expert advisers who have given the undertaking and are permitted to remain) (Rule 24).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protects commercially sensitive information during testimony while limiting access to counsel/approved experts who have undertaken not to disclose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Access to confidential material by counsel and experts with undertakings
rubrics_metrics.description: Confidential briefs, documents and exhibits are made available by the Tribunal only to counsel who are appearing for parties represented at the hearings, and those counsel are required to give an undertaking not to reveal confidential information to their clients. Expert advisers to counsel — accountants, for example — may be given access to confidential information at the Tribunal's discretion and with the consent of other parties. In-house counsel and board members are not given access.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strict limits on dissemination of confidential material; counsel must protect confidentiality even from their own clients unless permitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Witness procedure: written statements followed by examination (Rule 19)
rubrics_metrics.description: Most of the first day is taken by all the witnesses (who are sworn in) reading prepared statements into the record; following this, examination-in-chief and cross-examination proceed, often for several days, followed by final argument. This practice replaced lengthy Q&A to inject order and shorten proceedings (Rule 19).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structured witness procedure intended to make hearings more orderly and efficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subpoena power and documentary requests (Rule 20)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Tribunal has the power of subpoena, and any person who has filed a Notice of Appearance may have the Secretary subpoena any person (Rule 20). Subpoenas are sometimes issued at the request of interested parties. The Tribunal often invites testimony of persons not adversarially involved and requests original documents in support of information; such requests have never been refused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanism to secure witnesses and original documentary evidence; in practice Tribunal's informal requests have sufficed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tribunal builds its own case for injury (independence from Deputy Minister's injury info)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Tribunal builds the case for injury afresh and takes no cognizance of information on injury assembled by National Revenue, because that information is obtained administratively and not critically tested by adverse parties; to base quasi-judicial findings on such information would invite appeals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensures adversarial testing of injury evidence; but leads to duplication of research and potential inefficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Deputy Minister's dumping margin information in Tribunal deliberations
rubrics_metrics.description: Information provided by the Deputy Minister on the margin of dumping is received into the record, made available in confidence to counsel, and considered by the Tribunal in reaching its decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the Tribunal avoids 'looking behind' preliminary determinations, it accepts margin figures as part of the record and uses them when assessing plausibility of material injury findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: No jurisdiction to 'look behind' preliminary determination of dumping
rubrics_metrics.description: The Tribunal refused to 'look behind' the preliminary determination, arguing nothing in the Act gives it jurisdiction 'to sit in appeal on the issue of dumping' and that the Act establishes a 'basic dichotomy of functions...'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tribunal's role is limited to injury; challenges to the Deputy Minister's dumping methods are not within the Tribunal's appeal jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Reciprocity" rule and its limits (Rule 23)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule 23 states that 'the Tribunal may disregard as evidence any brief, written submission or exhibit received prior to or during the course of an inquiry unless the person or his representative who filed the brief, submission or exhibit is present at the hearing to testify to the matters set out in the brief, exhibit or submission'. This practice prevented full access by counsel to confidential information when the provider was not represented at the hearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Application of reciprocity led to errors (Steam traps) and was adjusted so Tribunal now makes confidential information available in confidence to counsel even if provider not represented; Rule 23 still permits disregarding evidence that cannot be tested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of acting on undisclosed information and granting adjournments
rubrics_metrics.description: Tribunal must not act on information not disclosed to the parties with the result that an applicant has no opportunity to respond; refusal to grant adjournment to allow response is improper (Steam traps decision).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Magnasonic and Steam traps decisions require Tribunal to disclose information or disregard it; fairness may require adjournment when new material is revealed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final Staff Report and members' meetings to reach consensus
rubrics_metrics.description: After the hearing, the researcher prepares the Final Staff Report incorporating additional information produced during the hearing; within days another members' meeting is held to discuss the case and attempt to reach a consensus on the finding and reasons. One member writes a draft reasons which may be edited by researcher and an editor for stylistic/grammatical changes, all within the 90-day time limit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structured internal process for drafting reasons and achieving panel consensus under tight statutory deadline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication and availability of findings and reasons (Rule 25)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Tribunal's finding and reasons are sent by mail to those who were sent the Notice of Commencement and to other interested parties, and are published in the Canada Gazette (Rule 25). Statements of reasons are not published, but are available on request.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Findings are publicly announced; reasons are not routinely published though made available on request — recommendation that Tribunal publish 'information obtained' for transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation to publish 'information obtained' (transparency)
rubrics_metrics.description: It would be useful if the Anti-dumping Tribunal made public such information as the United States International Trade Commission did when it issued 'information obtained' in its investigation — including sales at LTFV, marketing, channels, consumption, shipments, imports, practices and profits, profit-and-loss, and statistical tables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishing 'information obtained' would improve external understanding of Tribunal operations and reasoning and reduce reliance on confidential transcript access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 13 reference procedure (subsection 13(8) and Rules 3-6)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 13 provides for reference of the injury question to the Tribunal prior to a preliminary determination; subsection 13(8) requires the Tribunal to 'render its advice on the question as soon as possible, without holding any hearings thereon, on the basis of such information and advice as is then available to it'. Rules 3-6 deal with mechanics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fast, advice-only reference mechanism based on available information; hearings are not required under subsection 13(8).

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 16(1) economic inquiry procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Subsection 16(1) authorizes the Tribunal to inquire into and report on matters referred by Governor in Council relating to imports that may cause or threaten injury. Rule 26 requires issuance of Notice of Commencement; Rule 27 states Tribunal is not bound by other Rules during a section 16.1 inquiry, though it generally follows normal procedure; Magnasonic is not relevant to section 16.1 inquiries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinct inquiry function for broader economic matters; procedural flexibility during such inquiries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 31 review and Rule 28-30 review mechanics
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 31 provides Tribunal may review, rescind, change, alter or vary an order or finding or re-hear any matter. Rule 28 allows any person affected to apply for review stating grounds. If sufficient grounds, Rule 29 publishes Notice of Review. Rule 30 requires notifying interested parties and permitting oral or written representations if proposing to change an order or finding. Tribunal not bound by other Rules during reviews though practice is to hold pre-hearing and formal hearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review mechanism enables correction/modification of prior Tribunal decisions; practice shows many reviews result in change or rescission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final determination steps and appeals
rubrics_metrics.description: If the Tribunal finds no material injury, the Deputy Minister terminates proceedings and refunds provisional duty. If the Tribunal finds material injury or retardation, the Deputy Minister reinvestigates normal or export price to establish a definitive margin; final determination leads to assessment of anti-dumping duties; amount applicable to provisionally entered goods may not exceed provisional duty paid. The final determination may be appealed to the Tariff Board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines post-Tribunal administrative steps, caps on retrospective duty, and appeal path to Tariff Board.

rubrics_metrics.name: Redetermination, reappraisal, and periodic reinvestigation (Section 18 practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 18 provides for redetermination of description or reappraisal of normal value by a Dominion customs appraiser; appeal to Deputy Minister; and redetermination on initiative of Deputy Minister. Special Assessment Programs practice is to reinvestigate normal values and export prices about once a year so values reflect changes in expenses, costs and market conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanisms exist for administrative correction and annual updating of valuation bases to reflect market changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systemic assessment: dichotomy of functions causes inefficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: The Canadian anti-dumping system labours under two disabilities: an irrational dichotomy of functions (National Revenue investigates dumping; the Tribunal considers injury) and because of Federal Court intervention one function is treated as administrative while the other is quasi-judicial. These disabilities are responsible for defects in process and procedures, including duplication of research and inefficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique of institutional design; recommendation that Tribunal begin product study when Deputy Minister's investigation is under way to reduce duplication and improve preparedness.
